notes.title: Start here: one checkout use case, read in a fixed order
notes.body:
Netgum is a small .NET 8 shop for digital products. This quest is about one method pair in `CheckoutService`: `CreateSessionAsync` (start a checkout) and `CompleteOrderAsync` (settle it after the payment provider answers).

Read in this order:

1. `01-CODEBASE-MAP.md` for the layers: Api, Application, Domain, Infrastructure.
2. `02-CONCEPTS.md` for the ideas: preflight checks, one clock read, terminal states.
3. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md` for the before/after of the real code.
4. `04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md` and `07-TRACE-LAB.md` to see how the tests prove the ordering.

Keep `CheckoutService.cs` open beside the guides. Every claim in the guides points at a line in that file, and the quiz asks about those lines. The payment gateway and email sender are fakes, so nothing here is a real payment system.

excerpts.quote: The improvement is to validate deterministic input before an external gateway call or tracked entity mutation, then make paid and failed completion terminal and idempotent.
The Netgum request enters through `src/Netgum.Api/Endpoints/CheckoutEndpoints.cs`.

readMore.why: The one file the whole quest is about; read both methods top to bottom.
The dependency direction between the four projects.

notes.title: Core idea: a gateway call and a tracked write are side effects
notes.body:
Two kinds of step in checkout cannot be taken back cheaply.

- Calling the payment gateway can create a real charge intent at the provider.
- Changing a property on an object that EF Core tracks (stock, coupon count) marks it dirty, and the next save writes it.

So the guide sorts the work into "checks that change nothing" and "steps with effects", and wants every check first. A check that changes nothing is called a preflight. The domain classes gained small preflight methods for exactly this. When you read `CreateSessionAsync`, label each line as check or effect, and see where the first effect happens.

excerpts.quote: Deterministic validation belongs before the provider because a provider call can create a real charge intent.
Tracked aggregate mutation belongs after the candidate order is valid because EF is observing the same object that the test holds.

readMore.why: The original unsafe order and why it failed after payment intent creation.

notes.title: Core idea: Paid and Failed are terminal, and completion can be called twice
notes.body:
A payment provider, a retrying client or a user double-click can make the completion endpoint run more than once for the same order. The order has a small state machine: it starts Pending and can move to Paid or to Failed, and nothing moves out of those two.

Idempotent means: calling it again gives the same answer and repeats no side effect (no second provider status query, no second save, no second email). Read how `CompleteOrderAsync` checks the stored state before doing work, and in which order it does its reads. The tests prove this with counters on fake collaborators.

excerpts.quote: Terminal completion is a persisted state machine. Pending can become Paid or Failed.
Pending = 0, Paid = 1, Failed = 2,

readMore.why: How the counting doubles show that a repeat call does no extra work.

notes.title: Why the customer check comes before the product lookup
notes.body:
The key is right: line 38 calls `Order.ValidateCustomer(request.CustomerEmail, request.CustomerName)` straight after `var now = _clock.UtcNow;` and before `GetPublishedBySlugAsync`. Name and email can be judged from the request alone, so they are checked before any database work.

- `Product.ValidatePurchase` needs the loaded product, so it runs after the lookup (line 44).
- `Coupon.CanRedeem` is reached later, inside `CalculateDiscount` and again after the gateway await.
- `ProductVariant.ValidateReservation` is called from inside `ValidatePurchase`, so it also needs the product first.

excerpts.quote: Order.ValidateCustomer(request.CustomerEmail, request.CustomerName);
product.ValidatePurchase(request.VariantId);

notes.title: Why `now` is read once and reused
notes.body:
The key is right: the coupon is judged twice, once in `CalculateDiscount(subtotal, now)` and once in `CanRedeem(now)` after the gateway await. If each line read the clock again, a coupon could be valid for the discount and expired a moment later for the redemption check. One captured value makes both decisions about the same instant.

- No concurrency token exists in this code; `now` is stored as the order's `CreatedAt`, not as a row version.
- The guide gives consistency as the reason, not clock cost.
- The receipt email is sent in a different method, `CompleteOrderAsync`, which reads the clock itself.

excerpts.quote: The coupon calculation uses a captured `now`; calling `_clock.UtcNow` at each line could cross an expiry boundary.
!coupon.CanRedeem(now)

notes.title: ValidateReservation asks the stock question without changing stock
notes.body:
The key is right: `ValidateReservation` throws for an inactive variant and for stock at or below zero, exactly like `ReserveOne`, but it has no `StockQuantity--` line. That is what makes it safe to call before the gateway.

- It does not skip `IsActive`; that is its first check.
- No lock is taken anywhere; the guide says a concurrent caller can still change state between check and mutation.
- An inactive variant always throws "Variant is not active.", whatever the stock.

excerpts.quote: public void ValidateReservation()
`ProductVariant.ValidateReservation` exposes the existing `ReserveOne` rules as a non-mutating check.

notes.title: A null stock count means unlimited
notes.body:
The key is right: `ReserveOne` checks `IsActive`, then `if (StockQuantity is null) { return; }`, so a variant with no count is never decremented and never sold out. `ValidateReservation` agrees: the pattern `StockQuantity is <= 0` is false for null.

- A null count is not read as zero; the sold-out branch only runs for a real number at or below zero.
- Nothing sets the count to 0 here; the method returns before the decrement.
- `int?` does not throw on `--`, and the early return means that line is never reached anyway.

excerpts.quote: if (StockQuantity is null)
if (StockQuantity is <= 0)

notes.title: What a throw after the gateway call leaves behind
notes.body:
The key is right. `CreatePaymentIntentAsync` runs before line 59, so by the time the second `ValidatePurchase` throws, the provider already holds a payment intent. Nothing in `CreateSessionAsync` cancels it; the guide names compensation as a separate design. Everything else comes after line 59 (`Order.CreatePending`, `ReserveInventory`, `MarkRedeemed`, `_orders.Add`, `SaveChangesAsync`), so no order row, stock change or coupon change is saved.

A caution about this re-check: it reads the product this request already loaded and is tracking, so a sale made through another request's context is not seen here. The concepts chapter says the post-await check narrows the race but does not close it.

- No cancel call exists; the intent stays at the provider.
- `Order.CreatePending` runs only after both re-checks pass.
- `ReserveInventory` is also after line 59, so stock is untouched.

excerpts.quote: product.ValidatePurchase(request.VariantId);
They do not roll back a provider intent created during the await, which is why the code and course call out compensation as a separate concern.
The post-await `ValidatePurchase` narrows the race but does not close it

notes.title: The Failed check comes first, before any read
notes.body:
The key is right: lines 102-105 return `ToReceipt(order, "Unknown product")` as soon as the stored status is Failed. The product query (line 107) and the provider status call (line 114) are below that return, so a repeat call does neither.

- No second status call or save happens; the guide and the tests count exactly one status query.
- `MarkPaymentFailed` is not called again, and if it were it would throw "Only pending orders can fail payment."
- The product is not loaded on this branch at all; the failed receipt says "Unknown product".

excerpts.quote: if (order.PaymentStatus == PaymentStatus.Failed)
throw new DomainException("Only pending orders can fail payment.");

notes.title: Where the paid receipt gets its product name
notes.body:
The key is right: line 108 is `var productName = product?.Name ?? "Purchased product";`. If the product lookup returns null, the paid receipt says "Purchased product".

- "Unknown product" is used only on the failed branches.
- `Order` has no product name property; the debugging guide says product name is not persisted on Order.
- `ToReceipt` passes the name straight through; it never replaces it with an empty string.

excerpts.quote: var productName = product?.Name ?? "Purchased product";
remember product name is not persisted on Order

notes.title: Working the 46.31 total by hand
notes.body:
The key is right. Ten percent of 49.00 is 4.90, so the discounted subtotal is 44.10. The fee is 5% of that: 2.205. `Money.Create` rounds with `MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero`, so 2.205 becomes 2.21, and the total is 44.10 + 2.21 = 46.31.

- 2.20 would need banker's rounding (to even); the code names AwayFromZero explicitly.
- The fee is computed on `subtotal.Subtract(discount)`, not on the full price, so 2.45 is wrong.
- The fee is added to what the gateway charges: `subtotal.Subtract(discount).Add(platformFee)`.

excerpts.quote: Money.Create rounds 2.205 away from zero to 2.21, producing 46.31 USD total.
MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero
subtotal.Subtract(discount).Add(platformFee)

notes.title: The baseline did not compile at all
notes.body:
The key is right: the original catch block was `throw new DomainException("Email address is not valid.") from ex;`. `from ex` is Python. The C# compiler rejects that line, so the whole solution failed to build and no test could run.

- It did not swallow the exception; it tried to throw, in invalid syntax.
- It did not rethrow `FormatException`; the intended type was `DomainException`.
- "Compiled but dropped the cause" describes the first repair attempt, not the original. The final fix passes `ex` as the second constructor argument.

excerpts.quote: `throw X from ex` is Python syntax, not C#; the C# compiler rejects it
throw new DomainException("Email address is not valid.", ex);

notes.title: Why the factory repeats a check the service already made
notes.body:
The key is right: `Order.CreatePending` is public, so any code can call it, not only `CheckoutService`. The guide says the constructor invokes the preflight again because a domain constructor must remain safe when called directly. Repeating a pure check costs little.

- There is one DbContext per request here; trust between contexts is not the reason.
- Nothing is cached; `EmailAddress.Create` parses each time.
- `ValidateCustomer` checks both: the blank name and then `EmailAddress.Create(customerEmail)`.

excerpts.quote: The production constructor invokes the preflight again because a domain constructor must remain safe when called directly.
_ = EmailAddress.Create(customerEmail);

notes.title: Why the tests keep real repositories in the path
notes.body:
The key is right: the guide says a mock that never loads a real aggregate could pass while `Include` or value-object mapping is broken. With EF InMemory and the production `ProductRepository` and `OrderRepository`, the test loads the product graph the same way the app does. Only the external edges (gateway, email, unit of work) are replaced by counting doubles.

- InMemory does not enforce relational constraints or SQL transactions; the guides say so repeatedly.
- `ProductRepository` is internal, but `InternalsVisibleTo("Netgum.Tests")` lets the tests construct it, which they do.
- No migrations exist yet; the architecture doc lists them as future work.

excerpts.quote: A mock that never loads a real aggregate could pass while `Include` or value-object mapping is broken.
Add EF Core migrations once the SDK is available.

notes.title: What a relational provider adds to SaveChangesAsync
notes.body:
The key is right: on SQL Server or PostgreSQL, `SaveChangesAsync` wraps every tracked change in one transaction, so the order insert, the stock decrement and the coupon increment all land or none do. InMemory applies them one by one with no rollback.

- Change tracking is a DbContext feature; InMemory tests already detect the changed `StockQuantity`.
- Identity resolution is also a DbContext feature, on any provider.
- No provider re-runs domain checks such as `ValidatePurchase`; that is application code.

excerpts.quote: InMemory applies them one by one with no rollback.
